speaker_role: independent counselor (founder of BlueSkies Ivy League Coaching)
commercial_incentive: Yes, channel/speaker runs a paid college admissions coaching business (BlueSkies)
key_insights: Cites Harvard's own litigation data (from the Harvard admissions lawsuit) showing applicants ranked in tier 2 of 6 were admitted at 89% early decision vs 74% regular decision, and tier 3 applicants at higher rates early vs. regular.

Cites a downloadable dataset (from 'Big J Consulting' site, per speaker) covering ~400 schools' ED vs RD acceptance rates, noting schools like Brown, Cornell, Dartmouth, Northwestern, Tulane, and Vanderbilt fill over 50% of their class via ED.

Explains ED advantage stems partly from self-selection (only qualified/committed applicants apply ED, including recruited athletes/legacies with 'hooks') and partly from yield-signaling benefits to the college.
Frames the ED-vs-favorite-reach-school decision as a risk-tolerance choice, illustrated with an anecdote of a student choosing Harvard ED over a safer Duke ED bet.
Distinguishes binding Early Decision (one school only, must attend regardless of aid package) from non-binding Early Action (can apply to multiple EA schools).

Describes Restrictive/Single-Choice Early Action at seven schools (Harvard, Stanford, Notre Dame, Princeton, Yale, Georgetown, Boston College) as non-binding but limited to one such application, created partly to let students compare financial aid offers.
States most merit aid is awarded during early rounds, so students seeking financial/merit aid may benefit from applying early.
Notes 'priority' deadlines are mostly used by less selective/rolling-admission schools and aren't equivalent to formal EA/ED programs.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker citing Harvard lawsuit data: tier-2 applicants admitted at 89% early vs 74% regular decision
Speaker citing Harvard lawsuit data: tier-3 applicants admitted at 29% early vs 13% regular decision (as stated, order in transcript reversed but both figures given)
Speaker citing external dataset: ~400 schools list ED vs RD acceptance rates; several (Brown, Cornell, Dartmouth, Northwestern, Tulane, Vanderbilt) fill over 50% of class via ED
Speaker: seven schools use Restrictive Early Action (Harvard, Stanford, Notre Dame, Princeton, Yale, Georgetown, Boston College)
notable_or_distinctive: Uses actual Harvard admissions-lawsuit tier data and a named third-party dataset to quantify the ED admit-rate boost, rather than just asserting 'ED helps' generically.
reliability_notes: Numbers are cited from litigation data and a third-party site but not independently verified here; speaker is a paid coach with incentive to emphasize strategic/insider-feeling tactics; some figures in the transcript are stated in a confusing order due to auto-caption phrasing.
